params.question: Fine needle aspiration cytology can reliably diagnose both papillary and follicular carcinoma of the thyroid.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is actually false. While FNAC identifies papillary carcinoma with excellent sensitivity, follicular carcinoma diagnosis depends on demonstrating capsular invasion — something only possible on intact tissue sections. That is why any Bethesda category IV result mandates surgical excision.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. FNAC identifies papillary carcinoma with over ninety percent sensitivity, but follicular carcinoma cannot be diagnosed on cytology because it requires demonstration of capsular invasion on intact tissue. A Bethesda category IV result (follicular neoplasm) therefore mandates surgical excision.

params.question: In a pleural effusion cytology smear, how are reactive mesothelial cells distinguished from metastatic adenocarcinoma?

answers.text: Reactive mesothelial cells form tight three-dimensional clusters with nuclear moulding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This description actually fits metastatic adenocarcinoma, not reactive mesothelial cells. Three-dimensional clustering with nuclear moulding is a hallmark of malignant epithelial cells in effusion cytology.

answers.text: Reactive mesothelial cells form flat sheets with small intercellular windows

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Reactive mesothelial cells, which line body cavities, form flat sheets with characteristic small intercellular windows. Metastatic adenocarcinoma, by contrast, appears as tight three-dimensional clusters with nuclear moulding.

answers.text: Metastatic adenocarcinoma cells show transparent cytoplasm on Papanicolaou staining

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Transparent cytoplasm on the Papanicolaou stain is a general property of that staining technique, not a distinguishing feature of metastatic cells. The key distinction lies in the cellular arrangement pattern.

answers.text: Reactive mesothelial cells display hyperchromatic nuclei with abnormal mitotic figures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Hyperchromasia and abnormal mitotic figures are features of malignancy, not of reactive mesothelial cells. Reactive cells retain orderly nuclear features and form flat, uniform sheets.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the distinction: reactive mesothelial cells form flat sheets with small intercellular windows, while metastatic adenocarcinoma forms tight three-dimensional clusters with nuclear moulding.
Well done. Recognising the flat-sheet pattern with intercellular windows is key to avoiding a false-positive malignancy diagnosis in effusion cytology.

interactions.label: Muddy-brown granular casts on urine microscopy are characteristic of which condi

params.question: Muddy-brown granular casts on urine microscopy are characteristic of which condition?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Muddy-brown granular casts form from degenerating tubular epithelial cells and cellular debris shed during acute tubular necrosis. Their distinctive appearance is a key diagnostic clue on urine microscopy.
Glomerulonephritis produces red blood cell casts, not muddy-brown granular casts. Red cell casts form when erythrocytes are trapped in the tubular protein matrix during glomerular inflammation.
Pyelonephritis produces white blood cell casts, reflecting the neutrophilic infiltration of renal tubules during upper urinary tract infection.
Nephrotic syndrome produces fatty casts and oval fat bodies, reflecting the heavy lipiduria that accompanies massive proteinuria. Waxy casts may also appear in chronic disease.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each cast type maps to a specific condition: red blood cell casts = glomerulonephritis, white blood cell casts = pyelonephritis, muddy-brown granular = acute tubular necrosis, fatty casts = nephrotic syndrome.
Excellent. Linking each cast type to its specific condition is essential for rapid urine microscopy interpretation.

interactions.label: Which combination of cerebrospinal fluid findings is most characteristic of tube

params.question: Which combination of cerebrospinal fluid findings is most characteristic of tubercular meningitis?

answers.text: Neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, and high protein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A neutrophil-predominant CSF indicates bacterial meningitis until proven otherwise. Tubercular meningitis produces a lymphocytic pattern instead.

answers.text: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, and mildly elevated protein

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern describes viral meningitis, where glucose remains normal despite the lymphocytic infiltrate. In tubercular meningitis, glucose drops markedly.

answers.text: Lymphocytic pleocytosis, very low glucose, very high protein, and a cobweb clot on standing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tubercular meningitis produces lymphocytic pleocytosis with markedly low glucose, very high protein, and a characteristic cobweb clot that forms on standing — a classic diagnostic combination.

answers.text: Xanthochromic fluid with elevated red blood cell count

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Xanthochromia (yellow discolouration) in CSF signals subarachnoid haemorrhage, not an infective process. It helps distinguish true haemorrhage from a traumatic lumbar puncture.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the four CSF patterns: bacterial = neutrophilic; tubercular = lymphocytic + very low glucose + very high protein + cobweb clot; viral = lymphocytic + normal glucose; cryptococcal = India ink positive.
Well done. The cobweb clot alongside lymphocytic pleocytosis and very low glucose is the hallmark pattern — recognising it clinches the TB meningitis diagnosis.

interactions.label: A patient has a low TSH and a low free T4. Which thyroid condition does this pat

params.question: A patient has a low TSH and a low free T4. Which thyroid condition does this pattern indicate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In primary hypothyroidism the thyroid gland itself fails, so TSH rises sharply as the pituitary tries to stimulate it, while free T4 falls. The pattern is high TSH with low free T4.
In primary hyperthyroidism, excess thyroid hormone suppresses TSH to near-undetectable levels, but free T4 is elevated, not low. The pattern is low TSH with high free T4.
Subclinical hypothyroidism shows a mildly elevated TSH with a free T4 that is still within the normal range. The thyroid is struggling but compensating.

Correct. In secondary hypothyroidism the pituitary is failing, not the thyroid. TSH is low because the pituitary cannot produce it, and free T4 falls because the thyroid receives no stimulation. This breaks the usual inverse TSH–free T4 pattern.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the four patterns: primary hypothyroidism = high TSH + low free T4; subclinical = mildly high TSH + normal free T4; primary hyperthyroidism = low TSH + high free T4; secondary hypothyroidism = low TSH + low free T4 (the exception that breaks the inverse rule).
Exactly right. Secondary hypothyroidism is the exception that breaks the inverse rule — both TSH and free T4 are low, which is why free T4 must be measured whenever pituitary disease is suspected.

interactions.label: A patient presents with jaundice and liver function tests show an AST-to-ALT rat

params.question: A patient presents with jaundice and liver function tests show an AST-to-ALT ratio greater than 2:1. Which condition does this ratio most strongly suggest?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In viral hepatitis, ALT is typically dominant with a ratio below 1. The hepatocellular injury pattern in viral disease predominantly raises ALT because it is more specific to hepatocytes.
Obstructive jaundice produces a cholestatic pattern with elevated alkaline phosphatase and GGT, along with raised conjugated bilirubin. The AST:ALT ratio is not its distinguishing feature.

Correct. An AST-to-ALT ratio above 2:1 strongly suggests alcoholic liver disease. Alcohol preferentially damages mitochondria (where AST is concentrated) and depletes pyridoxal phosphate (a cofactor for ALT synthesis), raising AST disproportionately.
In non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, ALT is typically higher than AST with a ratio below 1, similar to viral hepatitis. An AST-dominant pattern should prompt consideration of alcoholic aetiology.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: the AST-to-ALT ratio is the diagnostic starting point. A ratio above 2:1 strongly suggests alcoholic liver disease (mitochondrial damage + pyridoxal phosphate depletion), while a ratio below 1 with ALT dominant points toward viral hepatitis or NAFLD.
Well done. The AST:ALT ratio is the first interpretive step in liver function tests — above 2:1 points to alcohol, below 1 points to viral or non-alcoholic causes.
